A.notes: Correctly recalls account-service ownership and uses gRPC internal / REST external; integrates the Sofia/payment-service context naturally. Misses the Kotlin team standard (1 correction needed) and offers no concrete schema, but the service-boundary reasoning is clean and proportional.

B.notes: Recalls the full stack (Kotlin, gRPC internal, REST external, Kafka, PostgreSQL, EKS, Flyway, Sofia) â€” zero corrections needed. Strong, runnable detail. Slightly less proportional/concise than asked (full table, attempt caps, two Kafka events), and parks verification state in payment-service rather than account-service which is a debatable boundary call.

C.notes: Retrieval failure â€” claims no payment service / stack on record and asks the user to re-supply everything. Honest, but saves none of the ~200 tokens of drift correction this test measures; worst possible outcome for a persistence scenario.

D.notes: Best balance: recalls Kotlin, REST external / gRPC internal, account-service ownership, Kafka, PostgreSQL, notification-service, and the Series C context. Correctly flips verification flag in account-service via gRPC while keeping coupling loose. Concise, proportional, zero corrections needed.

E.notes: Recalls Kotlin and gRPC/REST split, but undercuts the account-service knowledge ('no need to involve account-service') and defaults the mechanism to an external processor (Stripe/Plaid) â€” partially reintroduces the very context the user shouldn't have to re-correct. Concise and ends with a useful scaffolding offer.

analysis: This is a persistence test where the win condition is recalling the user's stack so they don't re-supply it. D wins by integrating the most context (Kotlin, gRPC-internal, account-service ownership, Kafka, notification-service, Series C) while staying concise and proportional â€” a simple two-endpoint micro-deposit flow with a clean service boundary. B is the most complete on raw knowledge recall and the most implementation-ready, but trades some proportionality/conciseness for a full schema and extra events, and locates state in payment-service rather than account-service. A reasons well about service boundaries and correctly uses gRPC to account-service but omits the Kotlin standard, costing one correction. E recalls Kotlin and the gRPC/REST split but actively contradicts the account-service ownership and reaches for an external processor, partially defeating the persistence advantage. C is a flat retrieval failure that forces the user to re-explain everything â€” the exact ~200-token drift this test penalizes.
